before.scope_note: A selective teaching map of sociocultural anthropology and ethnography, not all anthropology. Evolutionary, historical, functional, structural, interpretive, feminist and critical inquiries overlap without forming a single succession. Chinese research, Māori scholarship and collaborative histories have distinct trajectories. These approaches and rosters neither establish exclusive membership nor turn anthropology into one transferable theory.

before.label: Quantitative history
before.description: Uses serial evidence, linked records, statistics and explicit models to ask different historical questions. Labrousse’s prices, Henry’s reconstructed families, Benson’s voting groups, Thernstrom’s mobility and Curtin’s slave-trade estimates extend beyond cliometrics. Fogel’s counterfactuals and North’s institutions represent distinct economic programmes; Gutman’s criticism shows that evidence and interpretation remain contested within quantitative debate.

before.label: Historical demography & history of the family
before.description: Combines related inquiries into population, households, childhood and intimate relations. Henry’s family reconstitution and Cambridge’s aggregate and household studies differ from Ariès’s historical concepts and Stone’s family interpretation. Pollock’s criticism questions evidence and sweeping changes in parental care. Lee and Wang’s Chinese population study challenges received Malthusian comparisons without making the field’s regional patterns uniform.

strands.title: Childhood concepts, conduct and evidence

strands.title: Marriage, intimacy and disputed change

strands.title: Chinese population and Malthusian comparisons
strands.focus: Lee and Wang argue for forms of population regulation missed by received China/West contrasts. Their fertility and marriage claims remain arguments to test against evidence and regional variation.

strands.title: Patterns, exceptions and explanation
strands.focus: Hajnal distinguishes late marriage from remaining unmarried, acknowledges regional variation and separates identifying a pattern from explaining it. Goody questions its uniqueness and the scale of comparison.

strands.title: Local monographs and collective sampling

strands.title: Population totals and family subsets

strands.works: One Quarter of Humanity (1999),86–90; Harrell review (2003),543

strands.title: Local evidence and collaborative reconstruction
strands.focus: Harrell’s collection brings local demographic studies together; Lee and Wang acknowledge Campbell’s contributions. A broad comparative argument still requires attention to differences among local sources.
strands.works: Chinese Historical Microdemography (1995); One Quarter of Humanity (1999), opening acknowledgment

outcomes.finding: Selected primary Lee/Wang86–90 gives the explicit delayed-start/long-spacing/early-stopping claim and fertility-measure distinctions. Harrell’s complete2003 review questions genealogical gaps, local-to-national extrapolation and inference of intentional timing, with qualified rather than definitive judgments. Campbell’s explicit contribution and Harrell’s1995 edited local studies add the research context.
outcomes.research_limit: Book selected86–90 OCR, imprint and opening acknowledgment only beyond previously checked openings. Tables/figures not visually collated, endnotes and underlying datasets not checked. Harrell541–544 complete but his tentative assessment is not numerical adjudication.1995 collection publisher description/contents only. Later review remains reception bibliography, not extended mapped chronology;2005/2008 debate not newly adjudicated.
